n: After the defeat at Hormah, Israel turned back into the wilderness as God had said and circled the mountains of Seir for many years — the long wandering.

f.g: Went around, circled.
The rugged mountain country of Edom, south of the Dead Sea.

n: Then, after many years, the Lord spoke again.
“You have circled this mountain long enough: turn north.” The time of waiting was over.
Israel would pass by the land of Esau’s descendants, who would be afraid. God warns Israel to be careful not to take advantage of that fear.

f.w: your brethren the children of Esau

f.g: Be very careful.

n: Do not provoke them, for God gave Mount Seir to Esau. God keeps His promises to other nations too, not only to Israel.

f.g: Do not provoke or start a fight.

f.w: I have given mount Seir unto Esau

n: Israel is to pay honestly for food and water — no taking by force.

f.g: In KJV English, food in general.

n: They can afford it, because God has blessed their work and been with them all forty years. They lacked nothing. A beautiful summary of God’s quiet daily care.

f.g: He has watched over your journey.

n: They passed Edom by way of the Arabah road from Elath and Ezion-gaber, then turned toward the wilderness of Moab.

f.g: A port at the northern tip of the Gulf of Aqaba, near Ezion-gaber.
The Arabah, the rift valley south of the Dead Sea.

n: God also told them not to harass Moab, because He had given Ar to Lot’s descendants.

f.g: A Moabite city or region; here it stands for Moab’s land.

n: A historical note follows (verses 10–12): Moab had once been inhabited by the Emim, a large, tall people.

f.g: Emim — perhaps “terrors”; an early people of the region (Genesis 14:5).

n: Like the Anakim, they were considered giants — the Moabites called them Emim.

f.g: Regarded, considered.

n: The Horites once lived in Seir before Esau’s descendants displaced them. The point: God gives lands to peoples, as He was giving Canaan to Israel.

f.g: Horites, early inhabitants of Seir (Genesis 36:20-30).
In earlier times.

n: Moses resumes: God told them to cross the brook Zered, Moab’s southern border, and they did.
It had been thirty-eight years since Kadesh-barnea. By then the generation of soldiers who refused to enter had died, exactly as God had sworn.

f.g: Died off, passed away.

n: The Lord’s hand was against them until they were all gone. God’s word, even His warnings, never fails.
When the last of those warriors had died,
the Lord spoke to Moses again. A new chapter begins with a new generation.
Israel was now to pass by Ar on Moab’s border.
Approaching Ammon, they must not provoke them either, for God gave Ammon to Lot’s descendants as well.
Another historical aside (verses 20–23): Ammon’s land had also once belonged to giants, whom the Ammonites called Zamzummim.

f.g: Zamzummim — an early people, possibly the same as the Zuzim of Genesis 14:5.

n: They were tall like the Anakim, but the Lord destroyed them before the Ammonites, who settled in their place.
Just as He did for Esau’s descendants against the Horites. If God could do this for these nations, He could surely do it for Israel.
The Avim, who lived in villages as far as Gaza, were displaced by the Caphtorim — likely the Philistines, who came from Caphtor (Crete).

f.g: Usually identified with Crete; the Philistines came from there (Amos 9:7).
Gaza.

n: Now God commands them to cross the Arnon and take on Sihon, king of Heshbon. Unlike Edom, Moab, and Ammon, the Amorites’ land is part of Israel’s inheritance.

f.g: Fight, engage.

n: From now on, nations who hear of Israel will be filled with dread — as Rahab in Jericho later confirmed.
Even so, Moses first sent messengers with an offer of peace to Sihon. Israel tried peace before war.

f.g: A desert area east of Moab, later a Levite city (Joshua 13:18).

n: “Let me pass through on the main road; I won’t turn aside.”

f.g: The main road, probably the King’s Highway.

n: Israel offered to pay for food and water, just walking through.
As Edom and Moab had allowed — at least selling them supplies — until Israel crossed the Jordan.
Sihon refused. The text says God hardened his spirit — a way of saying God allowed Sihon’s own stubbornness to bring the consequences that delivered him into Israel’s hands.

f.g: Stubborn, unyielding.

n: The Lord said He had begun to give Sihon’s land to Israel: begin to take possession.
Sihon and his army came out to fight at Jahaz.
The Lord gave Israel victory over Sihon, his sons, and his people.

f.g: smote = struck down

n: Israel captured his towns and devoted them to destruction, leaving no survivors. This hard practice (ḥerem) is described in the book as God’s judgment on the Amorites’ long wickedness.

f.g: Hebrew ḥaram — to devote wholly to God, usually by destruction.

n: They kept only the livestock and plunder.

f.g: Plunder taken in war.

n: From Aroer on the Arnon gorge to Gilead, no city was too strong, for the Lord gave them all. The very walls that had once frightened Israel’s parents fell easily.

f.w: there was not one city too strong for us

n: Israel did not touch Ammon’s land, the upper Jabbok, or anything God had forbidden. Their obedience covered both what to take and what to leave alone.

f.g: forbad = forbade, prohibited
